h: Pakistan at a crossroads: shield for Riyadh or tangle with Tehran
dek: Christophe Jaffrelot asks whether the new defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey will make Pakistan the region's guard, or trap it between Iran and the Gulf.
body: Christophe Jaffrelot, a political scientist linked to Sciences Po in Paris and King's College London, turns this time to India's neighbour. In August 2026 Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact in Mecca, at a time when Gulf countries no longer trusted that America would keep protecting them.

According to the writer, Pakistan's new standing rests on three things: nuclear weapons, the showing of Chinese-linked aircraft and missiles in the May 2025 clash with India, and China's backing. Reports say it has sent 16 JF-17 aircraft, 8,000 soldiers and two drone squadrons to Saudi Arabia. But using Chinese weapons needs Beijing's nod, and a large part of the army is tied down on the borders with India and Afghanistan.

The real knot is Iran. Pakistan shares a border of more than 900 kilometres with it, there is Baloch separatism on that side, about twenty per cent of the population is Shia and half the gas comes from Iran. That is why Islamabad condemned both the American-Israeli attacks on Iran and the Iranian attacks on the Gulf. On the other side there is the pressure of money. In April 2026, when the Emirates asked for a loan of 3.5 billion dollars back, Saudi Arabia stepped in with 3 billion dollars.

Turkey, which supplies Pakistan with the most weapons after China, is the third link in this trio. On 26 October senior military and intelligence officers of the three countries met President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran, and there are reports that Iran hinted it would cut back its help to the Houthis.

Jaffrelot concludes that this pact could become the foundation of a new security order in the region, and also a trap for Pakistan. If the Houthi threat grows, Islamabad will have to choose: stand openly with Riyadh and anger Tehran, or give half-hearted support and get only half-hearted Saudi help in return.
nazar: In India, Pakistan is often seen only through the lens of an enemy. Jaffrelot's piece shows that it is also a weak country that lives on loans, the earnings of migrant workers and a neighbour's gas, and whose army is now selling guarantees for other people's wars. In the end the price of such deals is paid not by army officers but by workers in the Gulf and people in the border areas.
sawal: Can a country protect itself by selling protection to others?
ref: The Mecca pact
A mutual defence agreement signed in August 2026 between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.
Houthis
An armed movement in Yemen that has had Iran's support and has fought a long war with Saudi Arabia.
ank: Pakistani soldiers sent to Saudi Arabia
Saudi loan to repay the Emirates

h: Ladakh votes in the snow: convenient for the budget or for the voter?
dek: Sanjay Kumar and Arindam Kabir say holding the hill council elections on 4 December suits the administration's accounts, but could keep people who leave for the winter away from the vote.
body: For the first time, Ladakh is preparing to elect all eight of its hill councils. Until now there were only the Leh (1995) and Kargil (2003) councils. This year six new councils were created: Drass, Zanskar, Sham, Nubra, Changthang and Sankoo. After delimitation 100 seats were fixed, of which 36 are reserved for women. Voting is due on 4 December, and the panchayat and municipal elections come before that, on 21 November.

According to CSDS professor Sanjay Kumar and researcher Arindam Kabir, the debate is less about parties or campaigns and more about the date. Early December is the time of bitter cold in Ladakh. On 10 November the Kargil Democratic Alliance called a Kargil bandh (shutdown) over this and other complaints.

The administration's argument is the budget calendar. Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra says that if elections are held now, the new councils can draw up next year's budget by March; otherwise a full year will slip away. In his view schools stay open until 15 December and roads are better than before, so voting will not be a problem.

Those opposing it see a different picture. According to KDA co-chairman Sajjad Kargili, twenty to thirty per cent of the population, that is students, the elderly and traders, leaves in winter. MP Mohammad Haneefa Jan raised the same concern. The KDA also alleges flaws in the delimitation, and this fight is tied to the larger demand for statehood and the Sixth Schedule. Three Buddhist and village bodies have announced a boycott of the panchayat elections.

The writers accept that a year's delay would be costly for the new councils, but reaching voters is not a technical detail. A date that suits the calendar but not the voter weakens the very purpose of an election.
nazar: Since last year Ladakh has been asking for its own voice and its own government. Holding the first big local election on a date when every fourth or fifth person is away from home raises doubt instead of building trust. In a democracy the voter's convenience should come first and the office's later.
sawal: Whose election is it when half the people are not there?
ref: Hill council
Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council: an elected district-level body with powers over local development and budgets.
Sixth Schedule
The part of the Constitution that gives tribal areas rights over land, culture and local administration through autonomous councils.

h: A picnic at the airport: civic manners flow from the top down
dek: Retired Lieutenant General Bhopinder Singh says the decline in public behaviour is not only the doing of ordinary people, but also of leaders who teach entitlement rather than service.
body: A video went viral recently in which Indian tourists, reportedly in Vietnam, spread out food on an airport floor and held a group meal. Industrialist Harsh Goenka asked when we will learn to travel with manners. Many defended them, saying home food is part of our culture and sitting on the floor to eat is common in South Asia.

According to Bhopinder Singh, a former Lieutenant Governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Puducherry, the real question is not about food but about our failure to tell our own convenience apart from public responsibility. It is the gap between the lofty image of our civilisation and our everyday public behaviour, and the blame cannot be put on people alone.

The writer argues that civic culture is shaped by leaders, families and institutions, and what leaders say, praise and tolerate is what seeps into society. After Independence, Nehru, Patel, Azad, Rajendra Prasad, Rajagopalachari and Ambedkar disagreed with one another a great deal, but stayed within the bounds of the Constitution. In November 1949 Ambedkar said that constitutional morality is not natural; it has to be cultivated.

Today, the writer says, personality cults, grand events and leaders' pictures everywhere are spreading a sense of entitlement in place of service. Disruption in Parliament has grown and the language outside has turned more bitter. India Hate Lab recorded 1,165 incidents of hate speech against religious minorities in 2024, compared with 668 in 2023.

The moment we are criticised, we start invoking Ashoka's edicts, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family) and the drains of Mohenjo-daro. The writer says greatness is measured by how we treat one another and strangers, and how power is used. Pride is something to earn, not to show off.
nazar: Eating while sitting on the floor is no crime in itself, and such debates often turn into mockery of poor or middle-class tourists. But the writer's real point matters: when those at the top treat rules and courtesy as optional for themselves, that is the lesson that travels all the way down.
sawal: Does courtesy come from law or from example?
ref: Constitutional morality
Ambedkar's term: a respect for the rules and processes of the Constitution that even those in power honour, and not only out of fear.
India Hate Lab
A research project that records incidents of hate speech against religious minorities in India.

h: Naidu's second demonetisation: the first still has not been accounted for
dek: Seshadri Chari says that before any new demand to scrap big notes, there should be an honest review of what the 2016 demonetisation achieved.
body: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has asked the Centre to withdraw the 500, 1,000 and 2,000 rupee notes and keep only 100 and 200 rupee notes in circulation. He argues this will reduce corruption and boost digital payments. The demand came just as ten years passed since the demonetisation of 8 November 2016.

Seshadri Chari, former editor of 'Organiser', recalls that back then the 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were made worthless from midnight, and they made up about 86 per cent of the currency in circulation. The government had listed five aims: ending black money, bringing unaccounted wealth into the formal economy, increasing digital transactions, stopping fake notes and cutting off terror funding.

According to the writer, Naidu should first look at what happened to these aims. Accepting the demand for a second demonetisation would in itself be an admission that the first one failed, and since Naidu's party is a partner in the coalition government, that is politically difficult.

The figures speak for themselves. According to the Reserve Bank's annual report for 2017-18, notes worth 15.417 lakh crore rupees were scrapped and 15.310 lakh crore, or about 99.3 per cent, came back to the banks. So hardly any black money was caught, because it was held in land, gold, benami property and foreign accounts. Fake notes fell by about half, but the writer calls this 'using a cannon to kill a fly', and fake notes have come back. UPI and net banking also existed before demonetisation.
Chari concludes that the government should carry out a formal review of demonetisation, fix its flaws, and do so soon.
nazar: This criticism comes from a voice within the Sangh Parivar, which gives it more weight. Even after ten years there has been no official review of demonetisation, while the heaviest price was paid by daily wage workers, small shopkeepers and farmers who run on cash. A second experiment without an accounting would put the burden on them again.
sawal: How wise is it to repeat a decision that was never examined?
ref: Demonetisation
The central government's decision of 8 November 2016 to suddenly declare the old 500 and 1,000 rupee notes invalid.
Benami property
Property bought or held in someone else's name instead of the real owner's, to hide the source of income.

h: Pakistan's population: a growing burden that swallows progress
dek: An editorial in The Express Tribune says population growth has now outrun economic growth and must be treated as a national emergency.
body: Pakistan's economy cannot grow as fast as its population is growing. The paper reminds readers that the National Population Council itself has called this growth a national emergency.

The 2023 census counted the country's population at 241.5 million, and it is growing at 2.55 per cent a year. According to the editorial, this figure shows that the population question was never placed at the centre of development plans.

The results are visible everywhere. Public spending is falling behind the demand for services, millions of children are out of school, hospitals are not enough and there are not enough jobs to absorb the young people who come looking for work every year. The paper argues that even good economic growth cannot improve lives much when a large part of it is eaten up by the growing population.

Among the causes, the editorial lists girls' low levels of education, a lack of reproductive health services and poor access to contraceptives. It also questions the National Finance Commission formula, in which population alone gets 82 per cent weight in sharing money among the provinces. The paper wants this formula to reward human development, without punishing provinces with large populations.

As a remedy, the editorial calls for a national population stabilisation programme in which family planning services are easy to get and their results can be measured. The warning is clear: without decisive steps, the benefit of a young population will slip away, and pressure on education, health and jobs will keep hollowing out economic progress.
nazar: The most important point in the editorial is about girls' education and health, because every successful way of slowing population growth runs through giving women the right to decide, not through force. It is worth remembering for India too that this debate is won not with numbers but with schools and clinics.
sawal: Should budgets be shared by population or by progress?
ref: National Finance Commission
The system in Pakistan that shares tax revenue between the centre and the provinces. Its formula gives the most weight to population.
Demographic dividend
When a country has more people of working age. With jobs and skills it becomes a strength for progress; otherwise a burden.

h: South Africa: the wait for legal protection of relationships should end now
dek: Law professor Helen Kruuse says a plan to give religious marriages and cohabiting couples equal protection is ready, and Parliament should now turn it into law.
body: In South Africa, family law reform has been stuck for years in inquiries, consultations and drafts, while governments kept changing. Helen Kruuse, a law professor at Rhodes University, writes that the South African Law Reform Commission report released on 3 November now offers a way forward. The 'Protected Relationships Bill' it proposes would also recognise religious marriages and couples who have committed to standing by each other.

The need shows in the numbers. The 2022 census found more than 3.7 million people living together without marriage, and the registration of marriages keeps falling. The writer says the law should protect families as they actually live.

The history of delay is long. The commission's report on Muslim marriages was handed to the minister in 2003, a draft on domestic partnerships came in 2008 and a draft Muslim Marriages Bill in 2011, but none became a full law. In 2017 the writer's students wrote to the Minister of Home Affairs describing the helplessness of women trapped in religious marriages and partnerships; no reply has come to this day.

Meanwhile the courts kept making a path. The Constitutional Court's Bwanya judgment gave life partners the right to inheritance and maintenance, and the 2024 Divorce Amendment Act gave some protection in Muslim marriages. But according to Kruuse, rights should not depend on whether someone could afford a lawyer or the cost of a court case.

The proposed framework brings all kinds of relationships under one umbrella, without asking anyone to give up their faith or customs. In unregistered relationships the court will look at things like commitment to each other, financial dependence, care of children and housework. The writer accepts that many questions are still hard, such as whether couples can choose to stay outside this framework, but the aim of the debate should be to make a law, not to put it off.
nazar: In India too, the debate on live-in relationships and personal law often depends on the courts. South Africa's proposal shows that a shared framework can protect the weaker partner, who is mostly a woman, without binding everyone to one ritual.
sawal: Without a marriage certificate, what proves a commitment?
ref: The Bwanya judgment
A ruling of South Africa's Constitutional Court that gave a permanent partner outside marriage the right to inheritance and maintenance.
Law Reform Commission
A statutory body in South Africa that reviews laws and gives the government proposals and drafts for reform.

h: Poland's war over its court, and Moscow gains
dek: Political scientist Mateusz Piotrowski argues that the fight between the two big camps over the Constitutional Tribunal is breaking public trust, and this is just what Putin wants.
body: Poland's two big political camps are locked in a fight for control of the Constitutional Tribunal, and both are invoking the rule of law. According to the writer, this is lowering the standing of the state in the eyes of the public.

The quarrel goes back to 2015, when the outgoing Civic Platform parliament tried to fill seats that were meant to be left for the new parliament. Then the Law and Justice government used this as an excuse to pack the court with its own people. Now Civic Platform is back in power, but President Karol Nawrocki and the Tribunal's leadership are blocking the new judges. Last month a new judge suspended the Tribunal's president and vice-president, and police were sent into the building. The President called it a forcible takeover; Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it the restoration of the rule of law.

The writer says the roles have been reversed. The party that was once guilty of packing the court is now shouting rule-of-law slogans in the streets, and yesterday's protesters are standing with riot police today. Ordinary people are tired of this tug of war; they worry more about prices and security, because a war is going on next door.

Russia did not miss the chance. On 3 November Dmitry Medvedev called this move a coup. The writer points to Romania, where the presidential election was cancelled in December 2024 over charges of foreign interference, and warns that when the establishment in Eastern Europe starts overturning election results and the opposition starts calling the state itself illegitimate, the space for democracy shrinks.

His real worry is that people will stop seeing the institutions of the state as their own. On one side, social media under foreign influence stirs up distrust; on the other, those in power bend the courts and rule in the name of exceptions. According to the writer, this cycle weakens Poland, and there is little hope that the current parties will cure it.
nazar: This piece is a reminder that the independence of courts is not a matter of one party winning or losing. When every government starts seating judges to suit itself, the loss is to the trust without which any constitution is just paper.
sawal: When does a win over judges' seats become someone's loss?
ref: Constitutional Tribunal
Poland's court that decides whether laws are in line with the Constitution.
Law and Justice
Poland's right-wing party, which ran the government from 2015 to 2023. President Nawrocki is linked to this camp.

h: Four-day siege in Kulgam, hundreds detained
dek: After an attack on a CRPF checkpoint, search operations in the villages of south Kashmir have brought back memories of the 1990s.
body: On 11 November a CRPF checkpoint in the Akhran area of Kulgam, about two kilometres from the Jammu-Srinagar highway, was attacked and three personnel were injured. According to the initial probe, three armed men came on foot through a marshy route, opened fire and escaped. The NIA has recovered a mobile phone, a SIM card and cartridges from the spot.

After this, the cordon and search operation in the district went on for a fourth day on 14 November. According to The Wire's report, about 500 people were detained for questioning, and many of them were sent to Mattan jail in Anantnag under preventive detention laws. A senior police officer put the number at 300. Police also raided more than 200 places linked to people associated with the banned Jamaat-e-Islami.

Roads to several villages were sealed, people were told to stay indoors, and orchards and homes were searched with sniffer dogs. Videos showed vehicles being stopped and passengers searched, and men being made to lift their pherans (long woollen cloaks). Police say students and patients were allowed to move. Police have blamed the attack on a 22-year-old local carpenter and two foreign associates.
nazar: Catching the attackers is necessary, but putting a whole area under suspicion is the same old method that widened the trust gap in the Valley. Locking up hundreds of people under preventive laws looks less like investigation and more like collective punishment. The name of every person detained, the reason and the length of detention should be made public.
sawal: Why should a whole district pay the price for one attack?
ref: CASO
Cordon and search operation. Security forces seal off an area and search it house by house.
Overground worker
Police language for people suspected of giving militants supplies, shelter or information.

h: Smoke in Parliament: still no bail after three years
dek: A special court in Delhi has rejected the second bail pleas of Manoranjan D. and Sagar Sharma in the 2023 Parliament security breach case.
body: Manoranjan D. and Sagar Sharma, accused of jumping into the Lok Sabha chamber from the visitors' gallery on 13 December 2023 and opening canisters of coloured smoke, have not been granted bail. Special NIA judge Kiran Bansal said there are solid grounds to believe the charges against them are prima facie true. Both have been in jail since 14 December 2023.

The defence argued that the investigation is complete, one main and four supplementary chargesheets have been filed, and the trial is still at the stage of framing charges and will take a long time. They said coloured smoke is not a terrorist act, so the UAPA does not apply at all. They also sought parity with co-accused Neelam Ranolia and Mahesh Kumawat, who got bail from the High Court in July 2025.

The court said those two were in a different position, since one stayed outside Parliament and the other was not in Delhi that day. The judge cited Section 43D(5) of the UAPA and said that delay in the trial alone cannot lift this bar, though constitutional courts can do so on the basis of the K.A. Najeeb judgment.
nazar: The breach of Parliament's security was a serious matter, but treating a smoke canister as terrorism and keeping people in jail for three years without trial shows the same problem with the UAPA that even the Supreme Court has worried about. When the law ties the hands of lower courts, the delay itself becomes the punishment.
sawal: How much jail is fair before a trial even begins?
ref: Section 43D(5), UAPA
Under this, bail cannot be given if the court finds the charges prima facie true. That is why bail is so hard under the UAPA.
The K.A. Najeeb judgment
A 2021 Supreme Court ruling that said constitutional courts can grant bail even under the UAPA when there is long imprisonment and delay in the trial.

h: The DJ's noise moves on, the way of measuring it stays put
dek: Current rules and monitoring simply fail to capture the noise from DJs on moving processions.
body: In the season of weddings and festivals, DJs loaded on vehicles pass through entire neighbourhoods. According to this Down To Earth report, a reading taken at one spot shows the noise only for a moment, not how long people along the route were exposed to it. The Noise Pollution Rules of 2000 rest on average noise (Leq) and do not count sudden loud bursts.

In a Guwahati study, peak noise at Panbazar on Diwali evening reached 121.9 decibels. In Pune during the 2025 Ganesh festival, average noise at ten places was 95 to 102 decibels, while the daytime limit in residential areas is 55 decibels. In a survey people complained of broken sleep, ringing in the ears, stress and headaches.

Experts suggest taking readings at several places with synchronised timing, so that a noise map can be made and it is clear who was affected and for how long. A lawyer pointed out that religious or cultural processions are not exempt from these limits either, and repeated violations should be seen as a failure of the administration.
nazar: We still see noise less as pollution and more as part of tradition. The rules exist and so do court orders, but the courage to enforce them vanishes when faith or politics is tied to a procession. The elderly, the sick and children pay the highest price.
sawal: Why should festive joy matter more than a neighbour's sleep?
ref: Decibel
The unit for measuring the intensity of sound. Every ten-decibel rise means ten times the sound energy.
Leq and Lmax
Leq is the average noise over a period, Lmax the highest noise during it. Sharp spikes get hidden in the average.

h: Two jihadist groups clash in Burkina Faso
dek: Fighting between groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL has made the northern Sahel even bloodier, while the government's grip keeps weakening.
body: Since early September, the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM and ISIL's Sahel Province group (ISSP) have fought one big battle after another along Burkina Faso's northern border with Mali. ISSP has claimed to have killed more than 200 rival fighters at Katchame and more than 400 at Gandaouri on 9 October. These claims have not been independently confirmed.

According to ACLED, a group that collects conflict data, there have been about 320 clashes between the two groups since 2019 and more than 2,200 fighters have been killed. The International Crisis Group says JNIM dominates large areas in the north, east and west of the country.

This year 4.5 million people in the country need humanitarian aid. In 2025 political violence in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger took more than ten thousand lives. Analysts say the infighting may give the government some relief, but there is little hope of a lasting gain, because the violence is spreading to Togo, Benin and Nigeria.
nazar: This war in the Sahel rarely finds space in world news, though millions there are homeless. In the race between two armed groups, the villages that neither the government nor anyone else can protect are crushed the most. It is worth remembering that poverty, neglect and careless borders are the fuel of this fire.
sawal: When the state pulls back, who can villages rely on?
ref: JNIM
Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, the largest al-Qaeda-linked armed group in the Sahel.
Sahel
The belt south of the Sahara desert that includes countries such as Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

h: Called in for questioning, found dead in the police station toilet by morning
dek: After the death of a lorry driver held overnight at a police station in Madurai, several police personnel including an inspector have been suspended.
body: Balakrishnan, a 42-year-old lorry driver from Theni district, was found unconscious in the toilet of the Chekkanurani police station in Madurai on the morning of Saturday, 14 November. Doctors at the Government Rajaji Hospital declared him dead.

On 3 November he was carrying about 60 sacks of cardamom from Thevaram to Madurai when his lorry allegedly caught fire near Usilampatti and the goods were burnt. The company's manager complained that the sacks had gone missing, while Balakrishnan reported the fire. Police questioned him on 13 November, said there were contradictions in his complaint, and kept him overnight in the inspector's room at the station.

Police claim he may have taken his own life after inconsistencies in the complaint came to light. The family protested outside the station and asked how a man brought in for questioning was found dead inside it. Inspector Muthu, a woman constable and other personnel on duty have been suspended. According to the IG of the South Zone, the probe has been handed to the CB-CID and there will also be a judicial inquiry.
nazar: Keeping someone overnight at a police station without recording an arrest is itself a question. Tamil Nadu has a long record of custodial deaths, and each time the first explanation is suicide or an accident. Trust will come only if the CCTV footage and the post-mortem report are made public soon.
sawal: Which law allows a night in the police station in the name of questioning?
ref: Custodial death
The death of a person in police or judicial custody. In every such case a magistrate's inquiry and a report to the human rights commission are compulsory.
CB-CID
The crime branch of the state police, which is given the investigation of serious or sensitive cases.

h: Homes of those displaced by the 1983 riots torn down again
dek: In Assam's Lakhimpur district, the homes of 132 Bengali Muslim families settled there for forty years were demolished, while Hindu homes nearby were spared.
body: On Friday the administration demolished the homes of 132 Bengali Muslim families at Boginadi in Assam's Lakhimpur district. These families had been uprooted in the 1983 riots during the Assam Movement and had settled here on government grazing land.

According to Raijor Dal leader Azizur Rahman, the demolished homes stood on only about 9.9 acres of the 622-acre grazing reserve, while Hindu families living on the remaining 595 or so acres were not removed. He calls this a violation of the right to equality. He says the government itself settled these families here and also gave them roads, schools and electricity. Tushan Ali, 50, said two of his family's houses were demolished, but not the Hindu homes next door. Now the families are on the riverbank, and police are removing them from there too.

Scroll has sent questions to the district deputy commissioner; no reply has come yet. In the past month more than 1,900 Muslim families have been evicted in Assam, and over the past ten years the figure is about 19,000 families.
nazar: People once made homeless by riots have been made homeless again by the state forty years later. If removing encroachment is the aim, why choose by religion on the same piece of land? The pace of these evictions looks less like policy and more like an effort to keep one community permanently temporary.
sawal: How can one grazing reserve have two kinds of law?
ref: Assam Movement
A movement against outsiders from 1979 to 1985, led by the All Assam Students' Union, which ended with the Assam Accord.
Professional grazing reserve
Land officially reserved for grazing cattle. People living on it are often removed as encroachers.

h: Farmers in Jashpur's Loro-Dofa stop the Bharatmala survey
dek: Oraon and other Adivasi (indigenous) farmers say they want farmland in return for farmland, not cash compensation.
body: On Thursday, in Duldula tehsil of Chhattisgarh's Jashpur district, farmers of Loro-Dofa did not let officials who came to survey for the Bharatmala road project go any further. The road is to run from Loro-Dofa to the Ara area, and land of 32 farmers of the village is to be taken for it.

So far only two farmers have taken compensation; the rest have refused the amounts fixed. For instance, 15 lakh rupees has been fixed for about three acres of Ramprasad Rautiya's land, and six lakh rupees for about one acre of Sherafinus Ekka's. The farmers say farming is their livelihood and cash cannot take its place.

They demand an equal amount of farmable land in return for the land taken, and if that is not possible, that the project be moved away from their area. They also want proper notice before any further action. Their fear is rooted in the experience of National Highway 43, for which land compensation was stuck for about ten years.

Tehsildar Rahul Kaushik and Kunkuri SDOP Rajesh Kumar Sahu reached the spot with police and heard the objections. The tehsildar said a meeting of the SDM, National Highways Authority officials and the affected farmers will be held on Saturday to find a middle path.
nazar: Expecting trust for a second road from a village that waited ten years for compensation for the first is asking too much. If Saturday's meeting only talks about raising the amount and ignores the demand for land in return for land, the survey will keep getting stopped.
sawal: Can cash compensation make up for a livelihood from farming?
ref: Bharatmala project
The central government's highway scheme under which new roads and economic corridors are being built across the country.
Solatium
An extra amount paid on top of compensation for compulsory acquisition, which under the law equals the compensation.
ask: Give land for land, or take the road somewhere else

h: Alirajpur's Adivasis to march on foot to the Chief Minister against mining
dek: People of Guda and eight to ten nearby villages want a written order cancelling the land acquisition.
body: In Madhya Pradesh's Alirajpur district, Adivasi (indigenous) villages have announced that they will step up their fight against proposed mineral blocks and land acquisition. At a meeting in Semlaya it was decided that thousands of people from Guda and eight to ten nearby villages will walk to meet Chief Minister Mohan Yadav. The date and route of the march have not yet been announced.

Mahesh Patel, state vice-president of the Adivasi Vikas Parishad, said the Chief Minister had earlier assured them that Adivasi land would not be taken without their consent, so on whose orders were the district administration's two letters issued? Sarpanch Dinesh Devka and Guddu Devka said they had already put the villagers' concerns before the Collector at the public service camp in Guda.

The demands include a written order cancelling the acquisition and mining process, withdrawal of both administration letters, an apology for the Chief Minister's remark on World Indigenous Peoples' Day, and permission for a statue of Birsa Munda in Sondwa. The villagers say they want roads, schools, hospitals and irrigation, but not by giving up their land.
Patel also accused some BJP leaders of misleading the public with a 'fake' movement. The report carries no response from the administration or the government.
nazar: In a Fifth Schedule area, the question of land should be settled by the consent of the gram sabha (village assembly), not by an office letter. If the Chief Minister's verbal assurance is sincere, why the delay in putting it on paper?
sawal: Which will prevail: a spoken assurance or an office letter?
ref: PESA Act
A 1996 law that gives the gram sabha in Scheduled Areas the right to decide on land and resources.
Mineral block
An area marked for mining, which the government gives to companies through auction.
ask: A written order cancelling the land acquisition and mining process

h: Farmer leader Sopal Babuji placed under house arrest before Yogi's Meerut visit
dek: Farmers have been on a sit-in for 21 months against land acquisition for the Ganga Expressway industrial corridor.
body: In Meerut on Saturday, ahead of Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath's event, police held Kisan Sangharsh Samiti president Sopal Babuji at his home in Kharkhauda. The Chief Minister was coming to an ex-servicemen's honour rally at Kulwant Singh Stadium, and the farmers had announced that they would meet him and put their case.
In the morning police from Kharkhauda station reached his house and did not let him go out. Police called it a precaution, but gave no other statement.

The matter concerns the second phase of the industrial corridor proposed along the Ganga Expressway. About 800 farmers of Kharkhadi, Chhatri and Govindpuri villages are opposing land acquisition for it and have been on a sit-in at Chhatri Mod for nearly 21 months. They say the land is fertile and the compensation fixed is less than they are asking. Despite going to the administration and the government many times, no solution has emerged.
Sopal Babuji called the house arrest a violation of democratic rights and an attempt to silence the farmers. Farmers are angry about this action.
nazar: Farmers who have been sitting in protest for 21 months wanted to meet the Chief Minister, and in reply their leader was shut in at home. How will a government that is afraid to meet people find a solution through talks?
sawal: How did a wish to meet the Chief Minister become a threat to law and order?
ref: House arrest
Police stopping someone from leaving home without arresting them, often in the name of precaution before an event.
Industrial corridor
A strip along an expressway or rail line marked for industry, for which land is taken on a large scale.
ask: Stop acquiring fertile land, and pay compensation as demanded

h: Contract workers' protest at Telangana's government hospitals enters second day
dek: Sanitation, patient care and security workers are demanding a minimum wage of 26,000 rupees and warn of a bigger strike.
body: The protest by contract sanitation workers, patient care workers and security staff at Telangana's government hospitals continued for a second day on Friday. Protests were held at several institutions in Hyderabad, including Gandhi Hospital, Osmania General Hospital, Niloufer Hospital, Fever Hospital, Koti Maternity Hospital and Sarojini Devi Eye Hospital, and in the districts too.

The main demand of this movement, led by the Telangana Medical Contract Employees and Workers Union, is a minimum monthly wage of 26,000 rupees, which the workers have been raising for about two years. They also want the statutory minimum wage, paid leave and a bonus.
Senior union leader M. Narasimha said the workers have been working for very low pay for years and have not even received new uniforms.
The union has warned of a big strike in all teaching hospitals if the state government does not settle the pending issues. No response has yet come from the government or hospital managements.
nazar: Hospitals run not just on doctors but also on the people who clean the floors, push the stretchers and stand at the doors through the night. The silence on their two-year-old demand shows the real priorities of the public health system.
sawal: How many days can government hospitals run without contract workers?
ref: Contract workers
Workers the government hires not directly but through a contractor or agency, often on low pay and with little security.
Teaching hospital
A large government hospital attached to a medical college, where doctors are trained alongside treatment.
ask: A wage of at least 26,000 rupees a month

h: Bodoland minority students head to Delhi on 19 November against evictions in Assam
dek: ABMSU alleges selective evictions and demands rehabilitation and respect for the Constitution.
body: The All Bodoland Minority Students' Union (ABMSU) has announced a big protest at Ram Maidan in New Delhi on 19 November against the eviction drives under way in Assam. In Tamulpur, the union's president Taison Hussain alleged that minorities are being singled out in Nagaon, Goalpara, Lakhimpur and other areas, and thousands of people have been made homeless.

The union demands proper rehabilitation of the uprooted families and that every eviction be carried out within the bounds of the Constitution. Hussain said that if the government claims Bangladeshis have got into the NRC, it should give proof.

He opposed the proposed SIR and asked what will happen to the nearly 1.9 million people left out of the NRC, and whether the Citizenship Amendment Act will apply only to non-Muslims. He said minorities should stop being called foreigners, because this is 2026, not 1983.
Hussain also accused Dhubri MP Rakibul Hussain of not speaking up for the evicted families. The report carries no response from the government, the district administration or the MP.
nazar: Removing encroachments may be the government's right, but telling uprooted families where to go is also its duty. When doubt about citizenship is tied to eviction, the question becomes bigger than land.
sawal: Who has a rehabilitation plan before the evictions?
ref: NRC
The National Register of Citizens. Assam's final list came out in 2019, and nearly 1.9 million people were left out of it.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision of the voter list, in which every voter's eligibility is checked again.
ask: Proper rehabilitation for evicted families, and action in line with the Constitution

h: Sijimali mining protest: leaders in jail, families left alone at home
dek: At least 40 cases against those opposing Vedanta's bauxite mine, with bail stuck for several leaders.
body: The number of cases against people opposing Vedanta's proposed bauxite mine in the Sijimali hills of Odisha's Eastern Ghats keeps rising. According to Newslaundry's ground report, at least 40 cases have been filed. Five FIRs alone name 155 people and mention about 900 unknown people. These charges have not been tested in court.

Lakshman Naik, a leader of the Maa Mati Mali Surakshya Manch, was arrested on 16 October along with Dr Randall Sequeira. Both the lower court and the sessions court rejected his bail, and he is now preparing to go to the High Court. Hiramal, a farmer from Majhi Gaan village, first spent six months in jail, was picked up again in August 2026 and is in Bhawanipatna jail. According to his son, he was the family's only earner.

Lingaraj Azad, national president of the Samajwadi Jan Parishad, has been in Rayagada jail since March. His son alleges that every time bail moves forward, a new case is filed. According to the family, he has liver, kidney and diabetes problems.
This movement has been going on in about 40 villages since 2023. The Rayagada SP did not answer the reporter's questions.
nazar: When a movement is answered with cases against 900 unknown people, the aim looks less like investigating a crime and more like frightening villages. Blocking bail should not become another name for punishment.
sawal: Who is an FIR with 900 unknown accused meant to scare?
ref: Sijimali
A range of hills spread across Rayagada and Kalahandi districts, where Vedanta has been given a bauxite mining lease.
Unknown accused
People in an FIR who are not named; police can later add anyone to this list.
ask: We will not allow bauxite mining on the Sijimali hills

h: Drought after flood: half of a Beed village has left to look for work
dek: A second disaster within a year has hit Ambesawali in Marathwada, and people are heading for Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
body: Ambesawali village in Maharashtra's Beed district is half empty. By deputy sarpanch Dhananjay Gundekar's estimate, about fifty per cent of the village's farmers and farm workers have gone to Karnataka and Tamil Nadu in search of work. He would have gone too, if not for his duties in the panchayat. He had hoped for work paying ten to fifteen thousand rupees a month.

This is the second blow to the area in a year. In October 2025, floods in Marathwada washed away fields and standing crops. Now a long dry spell has withered the crops. On 26 September the state government declared drought in 265 of 364 talukas, or more than seventy per cent. This opened the way for relief in loan recovery and for water tankers.

Ganesh Ghodke of Kurla village lost six acres of land to last year's flood. This time he sowed cotton on 8 July. By September the plants should have been four and a half feet tall, but they did not even reach knee height. Many villages had no proper rain for forty to fifty days, and in some places the seeds did not sprout at all.

Suresh Tipale of Pargaon fears a loss of about ten thousand rupees an acre on his four acres. His tube wells have dried up. Mangesh Karpe, 32, of Kumshi had planted cotton on ten acres and hoped for a hundred quintals. Now even the two and a half lakh rupees spent on sowing is lost. He asks how the cattle will survive without fodder and water.

Government figures show that storage in 14 of Beed's 17 minor irrigation projects was below 25 per cent. 171 tankers were supplying water to 94 villages in four districts. Farmers fear that another failed season will deepen their debt, and that without help, migration will keep growing.
nazar: Floods and droughts are no longer news from different years; they fall on the same field in the same year. The relief system still treats every disaster as a separate event, while the farmer's losses keep adding up.

When half of a village leaves to do labour in other states, a drought declaration feels like a letter that arrived late. Only work in the village, water storage and timely crop insurance payments can stop the migration.
sawal: Who will add up the relief owed to a farmer hit twice?
ref: Marathwada
The central-eastern region of Maharashtra, with districts such as Beed, Jalna, Dharashiv and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar.
It is known as a region hit by drought again and again.
Wet drought
A state where crops are ruined by heavy rain or floods, for which farmers seek drought-like relief.
In Maharashtra this demand often comes up after floods.

h: Gaza Grad: a family that escaped the war, whose home is still Gaza
dek: A Palestinian father, a Russian mother and two daughters escape the bombing and piece together a new life in Russia and Egypt, but the wish to return never leaves them.
body: When war broke over Gaza in October 2023, the Ashour family stayed on as long as they could. The father, Ghassan, is Palestinian, the mother, Anna, is Russian, and there are two daughters, Liza and Dunya. For them Gaza was not a stopover; it was home. As the violence grew, they finally had to leave.

The family reached Russia and began living in Volgograd, once called Stalingrad, in the small flat of Anna's late grandmother. Anna had returned to the country where she grew up, but she brought her grief with her. For Ghassan, the hardest thing is leaving behind the life he built in Gaza.

Russia was not easy for the daughters. The language was strange, the ways were different, and the distance from loved ones hurt in its own way. Then the two sisters moved to Egypt, closer to Gaza, where the hope of return feels a little nearer. In this way one family was split between two countries.

The film does not dwell on scenes of bombing. Its question is what remains after your life is saved. The guilt of surviving, the loss of one's neighbourhood and people, and the small everyday things and habits that decide who we are: these are its real subjects.

Director Sawsan Qaoud is a filmmaker from Nablus who has documented Palestinian society through personal stories for decades. She studied television production in Russia and started her own production house, 'Mashahed', in Ramallah. Filming began in October 2023, when a small team in Gaza filmed the family in the early days of the war. After that, shooting went on in parts with the family in Russia and Egypt for about two years.

The film won the award for best human rights film at the 16th Karama Human Rights Film Festival in Jordan. It premiered at the Oran Arab Film Festival in Algeria and was also shown at the Thessaloniki Documentary Festival. Al Jazeera World presented a version of about 47 minutes on 11 November 2026.
nazar: News from Gaza often stops at the count of the dead. This film speaks of those who survived, and shows that the effects of war keep following people even after they cross a border.
The pain of displacement is not new to South Asia. From Partition to floods and dams, how the idea of 'home' stays alive after home is lost is the old question this film puts forward with new faces.
sawal: If your life is saved, is your home saved too?
ref: Volgograd
A city in southern Russia whose old name was Stalingrad.
One of the bloodiest battles of the Second World War was fought here.
Karama Human Rights Film Festival
An annual film festival held in Amman, the capital of Jordan, focused on films about human rights.
It is a well-known platform for this subject in the Arab world.

h: An imaginary letter from Nehru to today's Prime Minister
dek: On Nehru's birth anniversary, Manoj Kumar Jha raises questions of dissent, Parliament and pluralism in Nehru's voice.
body: On Nehru's birth anniversary, Janki Pul has published a piece by sociologist and Rajya Sabha MP Manoj Kumar Jha, translated into Hindi by Prabhat Ranjan. It is an imaginary letter: Nehru is writing to today's Prime Minister, who is not named. The letter says that more important than ritual tributes is how governments treat the ideas of those who came before, and that debates over history should not become an excuse to dodge today's responsibilities.

According to the writer, Nehru does not defend every decision of his own government and wants it to keep being examined too. Freedom did not mean only putting Indian rulers in place of foreign ones; it meant changing the relationship between the rulers and the ruled, or else colonial ways would carry on under a new name.

Dissent is at the heart of the letter. Even a big mandate is not a licence to silence the opposition. Concern is raised about the treatment of young people and women protesting peacefully. The writer sets out some tests: can a student ask questions without fear, can a journalist scrutinise the government without fear, and is a citizen who criticises the Prime Minister asked to prove their patriotism?

Here India's greatness is said to lie in its pluralism, and concern is raised that patriotism is being measured by religious identity. On Parliament, the letter says the government and the opposition are not enemies but partners; passing bills without scrutiny and suspending MPs hollows out Parliament. Critics such as Hiren Mukherjee are remembered with respect.

In the end 'Nehru' admits that power creates the illusion that an election win makes every decision right, and that he himself was not free of it. He promises to defend the Prime Minister's right to disagree, and hopes the Prime Minister will defend this same right for ordinary people.
nazar: Putting today's words in the mouths of the departed is an old literary tool, and its danger is old too: the historical figure becomes the writer's spokesperson. Still, the strength of this letter lies in its humility. Here Nehru admits his mistakes, and that is the rarest thing in today's politics.
sawal: Who, in the end, keeps the right to dissent safe?
ref: Hiren Mukherjee
A Communist MP and powerful speaker who was a sharp critic of the Nehru government in the early Lok Sabhas.
The Discovery of India
Nehru's book, written in prison in Ahmednagar Fort. It is an attempt to understand India's history and culture.

h: Chhath: from the village ghat to a tub abroad
dek: Ashutosh Kumar Thakur's essay looks at Chhath through memory, migration, vote politics and sick rivers.
body: On Janki Pul, Ashutosh Kumar Thakur's essay 'Suraj sabke liye ugta hai' (The sun rises for everyone) reads Chhath as something bigger than a festival. The writer, who comes from Madhubani district near the Nepal border, begins with the songs of Sharda Sinha, which in his words announce the festival's arrival even before dawn. For migrants, Chhath is not a holiday; it is the feeling of going home.

He describes the riverside ritual: women stepping into cold water, fruit, thekua and lamps in bamboo winnowing baskets, men standing nearby and singing. No idol, no priest, no walls; only water, sunlight and gratitude. That is why he counts it among the most eco-friendly festivals. In Mithila's farming society it was also an acknowledgement of dependence on the cycle of sun and water.

Then Chhath travelled out by train and in tin trunks. Ghats (bathing steps) are made on the Yamuna in Delhi, the Hooghly in Kolkata, makeshift ponds in Chembur and Borivali in Mumbai, Bellandur and Yelahanka in Bengaluru, and abroad in New Jersey, London, Toronto and Doha, sometimes in a steel tub, sometimes in a swimming pool. A second generation that has never seen the Kamala or the Ganga learns its parents' stories through this festival.

The essay does not look away from politics either. According to the writer, people from Bihar and Purvanchal make up about thirty per cent of Delhi's working population, so party banners compete at the ghats. The contradictions of urban Chhath are here too: polluted rivers, artificial ponds, plastic. He calls government clean-up drives mostly symbolic, and gives the example of youth groups in north Bihar who clean ponds and plant trees before the festival.
Writing from Bengaluru, the writer says at the end that since Sharda Sinha's passing the festival feels a little quiet, though her songs still play at the ghats, on rooftops and on screens.
nazar: Most prose written about Chhath stops at sentiment. This essay starts there and goes on to the state of the rivers and the arithmetic of votes, and that is what makes it worth reading. In a festival with no idol, where the river itself is the deity, a dirty river should be the biggest question.
sawal: In a festival whose deity is the river, whose responsibility is the river?
ref: Thekua
A sweet made of wheat flour, jaggery and ghee, the main offering of Chhath.
Sharda Sinha
A folk singer from Bihar whose Chhath songs have been the signature of this festival for generations.
photo_note: A painting of the festival in the Patna Kalam style, Sewak Ram (1809)

h: Muktibodh's bidi and a writer's own face
dek: Shayak Alok's fragmentary prose laughs at his relationship with Muktibodh and also questions himself.
body: On Hindwi's Bela, Shayak Alok's 'Roz-roz Muktibodh' (Muktibodh, day after day) is prose by one poet about another, but not in the polished language of tribute. It is fragmentary, playful writing full of self-mockery. It opens in a room late at night: the restless narrator finds a bidi (a thin hand-rolled cigarette) on a shelf and tells his companion that Muktibodh has arrived. Then the two jokingly 'worship' the poet and laugh at their own show.

The narrator sees himself as a bourgeois writer whom poetry alone cannot set free. The question of how a poem will give bread to a farmer standing in the cold stings him. When the power goes out he photographs a candle and calls it 'Andhere Mein' (In the Dark), admitting that photography is his artistic bias.

In later fragments there is a tree sunk in fog, a lover in a blue sari, and a reading of a Muktibodh poem to a Beethoven tune. A young poet's claim that you cannot understand Muktibodh without understanding Kishori Amonkar's music leaves the writer both laughing and coughing. He credits Muktibodh with the fact that broken, scattered lines are now accepted as poetry, and also mentions Shamsher.

The serious part of the essay turns inward. The writer imagines Muktibodh's face, his fatigue and his loneliness, and then worries whether this is turning someone else's life into the property of his own imagination. Where biography ends and where a poet's imagination starts claiming citizenship is a question he leaves open.

At the end come fathers and Agyeya, and the scene from Muktibodh's prose in which a well-dressed man at a tea gathering feels first pride, then shame and then loneliness. The writer links this to his own failure and the awkward performance of asking for favours.
nazar: Most prose about great poets is either worship or post-mortem. Shayak Alok tries a third way: he puts himself in the dock. Whether writing about a poet is devotion or self-display is a question that should be asked at every literary anniversary.
sawal: When does reading a great poet turn into building your own image?
ref: Shamsher Bahadur Singh
A poet of the Nayi Kavita (New Poetry) movement whose scattered, picture-like lines changed the craft of Hindi poetry.
Bela
Hindwi's prose platform, which publishes essays, memoirs, reviews and diaries.

h: Room 203 at the training institute, and a two-month world
dek: Abhishek Kumar Singh's memoir shows the friendship, gossip and theatre behind the romantic curtain of officers' training.
body: On Hindwi's Bela, Abhishek Kumar Singh's memoir 'Kamra number 203: ek samanantar duniya' (Room 203: a parallel world) tells the story of two months at a government training institute in the capital of a large north Indian state, where newly selected administrative officers come for training. The writer pokes fun at the romantic image of a government job: the car, the chair, the nameplate, the ID card. In his view the most romantic thing is the institute itself, green and full of rules, yet a place with no qazi (judge) or kotwal (police chief) to answer to.

At the centre of the story is Room 203, which the writer shares with a quiet, well-mannered companion from JNU. The two do not judge each other, and they protect each other's guests and privacy. Between tea and black coffee the room becomes a meeting place where officers come with their troubles like 'clients'. One topper sits on until four in the morning and skips class the next day.

There is a crowd of characters: a woman trainee about whom gossip flies, but who turns out to be composed and layered when you talk to her; Tiwari ji from Bilaspur, who seems imposing at first but turns out to love art and culture; a group across the corridor that calls itself 'Rajaji's army'; and a birthday party after which the two have to mop the floor in the morning.

The most interesting episode is on Gandhi Jayanti, when R.K. Narayan's novel 'Waiting for the Mahatma' is staged. Few people come forward, newcomers fill the roles, and the trainee playing Bharati keeps writing her own lines until the last day and makes the play better.

In the end the writer says that in that room there was everything and also nothing; uneasy people became easy and easy people became uneasy. He leaves without regret, because he feels he lived a whole lifetime in two months.
nazar: Most Hindi writing on the bureaucracy is either complaint or success story. This memoir catches the space in between, where the rulers of the future are still only young people: confused, talkative, lonely. What remains to be seen is how much of this room stays in them after they get the chair.
sawal: How much of the training room stays in an officer after getting the chair?
ref: Waiting for the Mahatma
R.K. Narayan's 1955 English novel, in which a love story unfolds amid the freedom movement; Bharati is its heroine.
Memoir
Prose based on memory, in which the writer records people and places they have seen and lived with.

h: Jahangir's jade cups: poison, power and poetry
dek: Fahmida Shahid explains how the Persian poetry carved on the Mughal emperor's wine cups dressed his addiction in spiritual robes.
body: Fahmida Shahid's piece in The Friday Times is the story of the jade wine cups Jahangir had made. It begins with a gold coin from 1611 that shows the emperor sitting cross-legged, raising a cup to his lips. According to the writer, for the Muslim ruler of a vast and diverse empire this was a bold statement. In the 'Jahangirnama' the emperor recorded his daily wine and opium with the precision of a pharmacist.

This tradition came from Timurid Central Asia, where a cup in the hand was a sign of conquest and rule. The cups were made of nephrite jade, which came along the Silk Road from rivers near Khotan and Kashgar in today's Xinjiang. It was believed that jade would crack or change colour if poison was poured into it. It could not be cut with metal, so craftsmen ground it with quartz sand or crushed garnet, and one cup took a year. The Iranian craftsman Saida-e-Gilani became head of the royal workshop.

From a literary point of view, the most interesting part is the poetry. Persian verses were carved on the rims of the cups, some by Jahangir himself, who was a good poet, and many by Sufi poets such as Hafez. In the Sufi tradition wine is a metaphor for divine love and intoxication for union with God. According to the writer, these verses covered the emperor's bodily addiction in spiritual language.

The English envoy Sir Thomas Roe wrote an eyewitness account of these gatherings. The cups that survive today are in the British Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and the RISD Museum in America; many reached the West through colonial plunder.

The ending is sad. Jahangir's hands began to shake so much that servants had to hold the cup to his lips, and he died in 1627 on the way back from Kashmir to Lahore. The very cups made to detect poison stayed filled with the thing that hollowed out the emperor.
nazar: In Hafez's verse wine is a metaphor; on the emperor's cup the same verse becomes an excuse. This piece is a reminder that power knows how to put poetry to its own use, and that even the most beautiful work of art can be a curtain over someone's weakness.
sawal: When poetry becomes a cover for someone's addiction, who is to blame?
ref: Jahangirnama
Jahangir's autobiographical journal, also called the Tuzuk-e-Jahangiri.
Hafez
A fourteenth-century Persian poet from Shiraz, in whose ghazals wine and the cupbearer are metaphors for Sufi love.
photo_note: The Passing of Shah Jahan, Abanindranath Tagore (1902)

h: The Rumi we quote, and the Rumi we forget
dek: Zamir Abbas says popular English versions have cut Rumi off from his Islamic and Sufi roots.
body: In The Friday Times, Zamir Abbas, an officer of the Gilgit-Baltistan government, asks how Rumi should be read today. Liberals, religious hardliners, atheists, musicians, self-help writers and LGBT activists all lay claim to this thirteenth-century Persian Sufi poet. According to the writer, in the West Rumi has often been turned into a quick cure for spiritual restlessness, and his free-thinking humanist image hides his Islamic ground.

The first argument is that Rumi should be read in the context of his time. He was writing within the Sufi tradition and learning from earlier poets and mystics. The 'Masnavi', with about twenty-six thousand verses, and the 'Divan-e-Shams', with thousands of ghazals, draw nourishment from everything: Bible stories, Hindu and Buddhist teachings, Greek myths, the Quran and the Hadith.

The second argument is that his thought is rooted in Islam. The fifteenth-century poet Jami called the 'Masnavi' the Quran in Persian, not in the sense of equality but of depth. By Abdolkarim Soroush's count, the 'Masnavi' has more than a thousand Quranic references.

The third and sharpest argument is about translation. The writer takes a famous quatrain from Coleman Barks's hugely popular English version, which speaks of a field beyond right and wrong, and shows that the Persian original clearly contains the words for Islam and kufr (unbelief), which Jawid Mojaddedi's translation keeps. He fears that if this softening spreads across the whole work, readers will meet a quite different poet.

His suggestions are practical: read reliable translations by scholars who know Persian. For readers in the subcontinent he names Shibli Nomani, Ashraf Ali Thanvi and Khalifa Abdul Hakim, and says that for speakers of Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi or Sindhi, learning Persian is not that hard.
nazar: What happened to Rumi happens to Kabir too: everyone picks up the piece that suits them. The writer's worry is fair, but there is the opposite danger too, of tying Rumi to a single religious frame. A good reading is perhaps one that avoids both.
sawal: Can translation evict a poet from his own ground?
ref: Masnavi
Rumi's Persian poetic work in six books, Sufi poetry woven from stories and teachings.
Coleman Barks
An American poet whose free English versions of Rumi sold very widely in the West.
photo_note: The meeting of Rumi and Shams, miniature painting
